 Waivers and extensions are different: BC Supreme Court sends film tax credit waiver application back to the CRA in Spell Love Road Productions 
 {A72573D5-E03C-4570-94BB-A8688E764345} 
 Regional Capabilities 
 November 20, 2026 
 On October 1, 2026, the Supreme Court of British Columbia released its decision in Spell Love Road Productions Ltd. v. British Columbia (Finance) , 2026 BCSC 1861. The Court held that the Canada Revenue Agency ( CRA ) acted unreasonably when it refused to waive the requirement to file a completion certificate for approximately $750,000 of Film Incentive BC refundable tax credits ( FIBC ) and sent the decision back to the CRA for reconsideration.
 Joel Nitikman, K.C. and Harry Cho of Dentons represented Spell Love Road Productions Ltd. ( Spell ). The decision demonstrates that a statutory prohibition on “extending” a deadline for filing a document does not create a prohibition on “waiving” the requirement to file the document in the first place, as permitted by subsection 220(2.1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) ( Federal ITA ). It confirms that a decision-maker must “grapple” with and respond to a taxpayer’s key arguments, particularly where the stakes are high.
 The FIBC regime
 Part 5 of the BC Income Tax Act ( BCITA ) provides refundable tax credits for eligible film and television productions. One of the requirements to claim the credit is to file with the CRA a completion certificate issued by the Minister of Tourism, Arts, Culture and Sport ( Tourism Minister ).
 Creative BC, a non-profit society, administers the certificate applications on the Tourism Minister’s behalf. It reviews each application and, if satisfied, forwards it to the Tourism Minister for review and signature. The applicant then files the certificate with the CRA, which administers the credit programme as agent for the BC Minister of Finance ( Finance Minister ) under a Canada-BC Tax Collection Agreement.
 Three provisions of the BCITA were central to this case:
 subsection 85(3), which requires the taxpayer to file the completion certificate with the CRA within 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the production was made;
 subsection 47(1), which incorporates subsection 220(2.1) of the Federal ITA into the BCITA; and
 subsection 47(3), which prohibits any extension of that 18-month deadline.
 Background
 Spell produced the film Color My World With Love in the taxation year ending January 31, 2023, so the 18-month deadline to file its completion certificate expired on July 31, 2024. Creative BC’s website recommends applying for the certificate at least six months before the deadline, but Spell submitted its application about two and a half months before. 
 The Tourism Minister did not issue the certificate until after the deadline had passed. As a result, Spell filed the certificate roughly two weeks late and the CRA denied the credit. To remedy the situation, Spell asked the CRA, as agent for the Finance Minister, to waive the completion certificate requirement under subsection 220(2.1), which allows the Minister to waive a requirement to file a prescribed form or document. The CRA refused, citing Spell’s significant delay as the reason: Spell applied almost two years after the film’s release, did not follow Creative BC’s recommended timeline and had received multiple CRA reminders before the deadline. 
 Spell then applied directly to the Finance Minister for the waiver. The Finance Minister responded that the request should be directed back to the CRA because, under the Tax Collection Agreement, the Finance Minister is bound by the CRA’s decision. The response also reiterated Creative BC’s service standards and its recommended timeline for submitting a certificate application. 
 Spell challenged the denial of the credit on three fronts:
 judicial review of the CRA’s refusal to waive;
 judicial review of the Finance Minister’s response; and
 a statutory appeal under paragraph 92(2)(a) of the BCITA of the Tourism Minister’s failure to issue the completion certificate in time.
 The decision
 The parties agreed that the reasonableness standard under Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov , 2019 SCC 65 applied. Justice Coval emphasized that reasonableness review must be robust rather than a “rubber-stamping” exercise, that a decision-maker’s failure to grapple with an applicant’s key arguments can render a decision unreasonable and that there is a “heightened responsibility” to justify a decision where the consequences for the applicant are serious. 
 The respondents emphasized Spell’s delay and relied on BCITA subsection 87(1), which requires the taxpayer to apply for the completion certificate “promptly after the completion of the production.” They also argued that a waiver would be inconsistent with the prohibition in subsection 47(3) on extending the deadline. 
 The Court acknowledged that the CRA had identified many factors properly against granting a waiver, but nevertheless held that the decision was unreasonable because the CRA failed to weigh those factors against those Spell raised in favour of the waiver. In particular, the CRA’s reasons failed to consider that: 
 Spell had submitted a complete and satisfactory application well before the deadline; 
 the certificate was issued within a few days once Spell reminded Creative BC that the certificate was late; 
 the waiver provision in subsection 220(2.1) is intended to relieve undue hardship, including the financial hardship Spell suffered in this case from losing approximately $750,000 in refundable credits; and 
 granting a waiver in these circumstances would not necessarily amount to an impermissible extension of the 18-month deadline. 
 On the last point, the Court distinguished waiver from extension, noting that a waiver was arguably justified in this case where the application was filed well before the deadline but not processed in time, particularly given the sizable amount at issue. The Court ordered the CRA to reconsider the waiver request, taking into account the factors noted above.
 Key takeaways
 The decision offers two main takeaways. First, waiver is not extension. Even where legislation prohibits extending a filing deadline, the remedial discretion in subsection 220(2.1) may still be available to waive a filing requirement. The CRA cannot simply treat a non-extendable deadline as a bar to considering a waiver.
 Second, decision-makers must engage with and respond to a taxpayer’s key arguments. A refusal that lists the factors against relief, without weighing the factors in favour and the consequences for the taxpayer, is vulnerable on judicial review, particularly where significant amounts are at stake.
